blocks.text: To begin the matter from its origin: the most ancient writers mention mice in Egypt and in Africa which have hind feet longer than their fore feet, and therefore walk on them as bipeds ^{(6)}. Herodotus, where he deals with Libya, book 4, chapter 192 [col. 1010]: Μυῶν δὲ γενεὰ τριξὰ αὐτόθι ἐστί. οἱ μὲν δίποδες καλέονται [Myōn de genea trixa autothi esti. hoi men dipodes kaleontai], etc. And there are three kinds of mice there. Some are called bipeds, etc. Aristotle, History, book 6, at the end: Οἱ δ' ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ μῦες σκληρὰν ἔχουσι τὴν τρίχα, σχεδὸν ὥσπερ οἱ χερσαῖοι ἐχῖνοι. Εἰσὶ δὲ καὶ ἕτεροι, οἱ βαδίζουσιν ἐπὶ τοῖς δυσὶ ποσί. τὰ γὰρ πρόσθια μικρὰ ἔχουσι, τὰ δ' ὀπίσθια μεγάλα ^{(7)}. γίνονται δὲ πλήθει πολλοί. [Hoi d' en Aigyptō myes sklēran echousi tēn tricha, schedon hōsper hoi chersaioi echinoi. Eisi de kai heteroi, hoi badizousin epi tois dysi posi. ta gar prosthia mikra echousi, ta d' opisthia megala. ginontai de plēthei polloi.] The mice that are in Egypt have hard hair, almost like land hedgehogs. There are also others which walk on two feet. For they have short fore legs and long hind legs. And they are many in number. Theophrastus in Aelian, History, book 15, chapter 26: Ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ δὲ ἀκούω δίποδας εἶναι μῦς, καὶ μεγίστους μεγέθει φύεσθαι· τοῖς γε μὴν ἐμπροσθίοις ποσὶν, ὡς χερσὶ, χρῆσθαι. εἶναι γὰρ αὐτοὺς τοὺς ὄπισθε βραχυτέρους. εἶδον τούτους. Λιβυκοί εἰσι. βαδίζουσι δὲ ὀρθοὶ ἐπὶ τοῖν ποδοῖν, ὅταν δὲ διώκωνται, πηδῶσι. [En Aigyptō de akouō dipodas einai mys, kai megistous megethei phyesthai; tois ge mēn emprosthiois posin, hōs chersi, chrēsthai. einai gar autous tous opisthe brachyterous. eidon toutous. Libykoi eisi. badizousi de orthoi epi toin podoin, hotan de diōkōntai, pēdōsi.] I hear that in Egypt there are biped mice, very large in size, and that they use their fore feet as hands. For these are shorter than the hind ones. I have seen them. They are Libyan. They walk upright, supporting themselves on their two feet. But if anyone pursues them, they leap. And from the same source Photius: Ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ [II, 421] δίποδάς φασι μῦας γίνεσθαι, καὶ μεγάλους. ἔχουσι δὲ οὗτοι καὶ τοὺς ἐμπροσθίους πόδας, ἀλλ᾽ οὐ βαδίζουσιν ἐπ᾽ αὐτοῖς. χρῶνται δὲ αὐτοῖς, οἷα χερσίν. ὅταν δὲ φεύγωσιν, πηδῶσι. [En Aigyptō dipodas phasi myas ginesthai, kai megalous. echousi de houtoi kai tous emprosthious podas, all' ou badizousin ep' autois. chrōntai de autois, hoia chersin. hotan de pheugōsin, pēdōsi.] They report that in Egypt biped mice are born, and large ones. They also have fore feet, but they do not walk on them; rather they use them as hands. And they flee by leaping. Pliny, book 8, chapter 37, after treating of the Alpine mice: there are also animals equal to these in Egypt (namely in what follows, since in other respects they are very unlike) and they likewise sit back on their haunches, walk on two feet, and use their fore feet as hands. And book 10, chapter 65: Egyptian mice have hard hair, like hedgehogs; they also walk on two feet, like the Alpine ones.

This kind of mouse, which is also common in Eretz Yisrael, the Hellenists therefore called ἀρκτομῦν [arktomyn], that is, bear-mouse, because it walked on two feet and used its fore feet as hands. For this is characteristic of bears. Oppian, book 3 of the Cynegetica, in his description of the bear:
Χεῖρες χερσὶ βροτῶν ἴκελαι, πόδες ἠδὲ πόδεσσι, [Cheires chersi brotōn ikelai, podes ēde podessi,]

Hands like the hands of men, and feet like their feet. Solinus, in the chapter On Numidia, and there on the bears: Their greatest strength is in the arms and loins; hence they sometimes stand on their hind feet.
